name: Heel Hook from Kneebar Control
summary: The Heel Hook from Kneebar Control is a leg-lock transition that converts a defended kneebar into a rotational heel hook, attacking the knee's ACL, MCL, and LCL once the defender bends their knee to escape the straight-line extension.
description: Learn the heel hook from kneebar control in BJJ. Complete guide covering grip transition mechanics, finishing details, defensive counters, and safety protocols.
target_area: Ankle joint, knee ligaments (ACL/MCL/LCL), and lower leg structural integrity
overview:
The heel hook from kneebar control exploits a fundamental defensive dilemma in the leg lock game. When an attacker establishes kneebar control and threatens knee hyperextension, the defender's natural response is to bend the knee strongly, preventing the straight-line extension that powers the kneebar. This bent-knee defense, while effective against the kneebar, directly exposes the heel for a rotational attack — creating a catch-22 where defending one submission opens vulnerability to another.

This transition represents a core concept in systematic leg lock play: submissions exist in chains rather than isolation. The attacker reads defensive reactions and redirects to whichever attack the defense creates. From kneebar control, the grip change is mechanically straightforward — shifting from arms hugging the leg across the torso to hands cupping the heel with rotational control — but the attacking vector changes dramatically from linear extension to rotational torsion against the knee's ligamentous structures.

The danger level escalates significantly with this transition. Kneebars provide relatively clear proprioceptive feedback, giving defenders time to recognize pressure and tap. Heel hooks attack the ACL, MCL, and LCL with far less warning, as rotational damage to these structures often occurs before the defender perceives pain. This makes the heel hook from kneebar control one of the most dangerous transitions in grappling, demanding strict adherence to safety protocols during training.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 months with surgical reconstruction, extensive rehabilitation
3-6 months for grade 3 tears, potential permanent instability

injury_risks.injury: Meniscus tear (cartilage damage in knee joint)
injury_risks.recovery_time: 4-8 weeks to 6 months depending on severity and treatment

injury_risks.injury: Ankle ligament damage and joint capsule injury
Tibial/fibular fracture from extreme rotational force

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW and progressive - minimum 5-7 seconds from initial pressure to maximum force in training. NEVER apply sudden rotational force.
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap with free leg
Frantic slapping or waving with hands
Leg stiffening or immediate defensive reaction
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure upon any tap signal
Release heel grip completely before releasing leg entanglement
Slowly unwrap leg configuration while maintaining awareness of opponent's joint
Allow opponent to extract their leg at their own pace
Check with training partner about their knee and ankle status
Report any joint discomfort to instructor immediately, even if minor
training_restrictions: NEVER apply sudden or explosive rotational force in training
NEVER practice at competition speed with training partners
NEVER continue pressure if partner's leg begins rotating with the submission
Always allow immediate tap access for both hands
Only train with partners who have explicit experience with heel hook defense
Prohibited for practitioners below brown belt in most traditional academies
Never train heel hooks without instructor supervision during initial learning phases
Stop immediately if any popping, clicking, or unusual sensations occur in opponent's leg

variations_and_setups.description: From inside leg kneebar control, redirect to inside heel hook by threading your near arm under the opponent's ankle and cupping the heel. The inside angle provides strong rotational leverage against the knee's weakest axis. Most effective when the opponent bends their knee deeply to defend the kneebar, bringing the heel within easy reach.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When your inside leg is the primary entangling limb and the opponent's heel faces toward your centerline

variations_and_setups.description: From outside leg kneebar control, transition to outside heel hook by threading your outside arm under the ankle and securing the heel with palm-to-palm or figure-four grip. The outside angle attacks different rotational vectors and can catch opponents who are experienced at defending inside heel hooks. Requires slight hip adjustment to align torque direction with knee vulnerability.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When your outside leg controls the entanglement and the opponent defends kneebar by turning their knee inward

variations_and_setups.variation_name: False Kneebar to Heel Hook Bait
variations_and_setups.description: Apply deliberate kneebar pressure with the explicit intention of forcing the bent-knee defensive reaction rather than finishing the kneebar. The kneebar threat serves purely as a setup — hands are pre-positioned near the heel during the kneebar application so the transition to heel hook grip is nearly instantaneous. This variation shortens the grip transition window that defenders rely on for escape.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against experienced opponents who know to defend kneebars by bending the knee but may not anticipate the immediate heel hook redirect

attacker.name: Heel Hook from Kneebar Control Attacker
attacker.description: Master attacking the heel hook from kneebar control. Grip transition mechanics, finishing sequences, common counters, and progressive training for leg lock chains.
attacker.overview: Attacking the heel hook from kneebar control requires reading your opponent's defensive reactions and capitalizing on the mechanical opening created by their kneebar defense. The bent-knee posture that neutralizes kneebar pressure simultaneously exposes the heel, and your ability to transition grips smoothly while maintaining leg entanglement determines the success rate of this attack chain. Mastery of this transition transforms your kneebar control from a single-attack position into a dual-threat platform where every defense creates a new vulnerability, embodying the principle that leg lock chains are won through reaction-based sequencing rather than forcing a single finish.
key_principles: Read the bent-knee kneebar defense as a direct invitation to redirect to heel hook — the defense creates the opening
Maintain leg entanglement control throughout the grip transition — never release legs to adjust hands
Overlap the attacks during transition by securing the heel before fully releasing kneebar pressure
Control the opponent's hip rotation to prevent them from spinning with the heel hook torque and relieving pressure
Apply rotational force progressively and slowly — the heel hook finishes with minimal visible movement but devastating structural force
Use the constant kneebar threat to dictate the opponent's defensive posture and keep them reactive
setup_requirements: Established kneebar control with hip connection to the opponent's knee joint and stable leg entanglement
Opponent actively defending by keeping their knee bent, confirming the kneebar is neutralized but the heel is exposed
Heel accessible to your hands — opponent's foot is not tucked completely behind your body or trapped by your legs
Leg entanglement is stable enough to survive the grip transition without the opponent extracting their leg
Clear identification of whether the inside or outside heel hook angle is available based on foot orientation

execution_steps.description: Continue applying genuine kneebar pressure to force the opponent into a deep bent-knee defensive posture. Pull their leg tight to your chest and drive your hips forward to maintain the threat. This is not a feint — apply enough pressure that the opponent must commit fully to bending their knee to survive.

As the opponent bends their knee to defend, observe which direction their foot is pointing and which side of the heel is accessible. Determine whether the inside or outside heel hook angle is available based on your leg configuration and their foot position. The heel should be within arm's reach without releasing your entanglement.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds of assessment while maintaining pressure

execution_steps.description: Reach your near-side arm under the opponent's ankle, threading between their Achilles tendon and calf muscle. Your forearm should contact the back of their heel with your wrist positioned to cup the heel bone. Keep your other arm maintaining the leg hug to prevent any extraction attempt during this transition.

Establish a figure-four or S-grip by bringing your other hand to reinforce the heel grip. Your near-side wrist cups the heel while your far-side hand grabs your own wrist or forearm. Pinch your elbows tightly together to lock the heel in place — any looseness in the grip allows the opponent to rotate their foot free.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds to lock the grip configuration

execution_steps.description: Shift your hips slightly to align your torso with the rotational attack vector. Your body should be angled so that a twisting motion of your torso and arms creates torsion at the opponent's knee rather than at their ankle. Tighten your leg entanglement to prevent the opponent from rotating their hips to relieve the coming pressure.

Squeeze your elbows together, pull the heel tight to your chest, and begin applying slow rotational pressure using your entire upper body — not just your arms. The rotation should come from your torso turning, transmitting force through your locked arms into the heel and creating torsion at the knee. Apply pressure progressively over several seconds.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds of slow, progressive rotational pressure

execution_steps.description: Complete the submission by continuing the slow rotational pressure while maintaining your leg entanglement. Keep your legs controlling the opponent's hip to prevent them from rotating with the torque. The finish requires minimal additional movement once the grip and angle are correct — small adjustments in torque are sufficient. In training, wait for the tap and release immediately.

common_counters.counter: Boot defense — opponent straightens leg forcefully during grip transition to prevent heel capture
common_counters.your_response: Maintain leg entanglement and return to kneebar pressure on the now-straightened leg. The boot defense re-exposes the knee to extension, allowing you to cycle back to the kneebar and force another bent-knee reaction.

common_counters.counter: Hip rotation — opponent rotates hips in the direction of heel hook torque to relieve rotational pressure
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation with your legs and maintain the entanglement. If they rotate far enough, transition to the opposite-side heel hook angle or redirect to a toe hold. Their rotation often exposes the opposite heel.

common_counters.counter: Grip fighting — opponent reaches down to strip your hands from the heel before the grip locks
common_counters.your_response: Secure the grip faster by pre-positioning your hands during the kneebar attack phase. If they commit both hands to grip fighting, their weight shifts forward, potentially creating sweep opportunities from the bottom entanglement.

common_counters.counter: Full leg extraction — opponent explosively pulls their entire leg free from the entanglement
common_counters.your_response: If the opponent fully extracts, immediately recover guard by inserting butterfly hooks or transitioning to single leg X-guard before they can consolidate a passing position. Use the momentum of their extraction to initiate a sweep.

common_errors.error: Releasing leg entanglement during the grip transition to reach for the heel
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their leg freely during the window when neither kneebar control nor heel hook grip is secured, escaping the position entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep legs actively hooking and controlling throughout the transition. Only your arms change position — your legs maintain constant entanglement pressure

common_errors.error: Applying explosive rotational force instead of slow progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Causes ligament damage before the opponent can tap, potentially causing career-ending ACL or MCL tears that could have been prevented
common_errors.correction: Apply rotation over 3-5 seconds minimum. The finish requires less force than most practitioners expect — slow, steady torque is both safer and more mechanically efficient

common_errors.error: Cupping the toes or ball of the foot instead of securing the heel bone
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient rotational leverage on the knee because force dissipates through the ankle joint rather than transmitting directly to the knee ligaments
common_errors.correction: Thread your wrist deep under the ankle so the heel bone sits in the crook of your wrist. The grip point must be the calcaneous, not the forefoot

common_errors.error: Abandoning the kneebar threat too early, telegraphing the heel hook transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the transition and pre-emptively straightens their leg or tucks their heel, eliminating the heel hook opportunity before it materializes
common_errors.correction: Apply genuine kneebar pressure until the opponent fully commits to the bent-knee defense. The heel hook redirect should feel like a reaction to their defense, not a pre-planned sequence

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's hip rotation before applying heel hook torque
common_errors.consequence: Opponent simply rotates their body with the torque, relieving all pressure on the knee and potentially escaping the entanglement entirely
common_errors.correction: Before applying rotational pressure, confirm your leg entanglement prevents the opponent's hips from turning freely. Squeeze your knees together and hook behind their thigh to anchor their hip in place

training_progressions.focus: Developing smooth grip changes from kneebar to heel hook without releasing leg control
training_progressions.description: Partner holds a static bent-knee defense in kneebar control. Practitioner drills the arm threading and grip change repeatedly with no resistance. Focus on maintaining leg entanglement throughout. 50 repetitions per side per session until the grip transition becomes automatic.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Chain Drilling with Cooperative Partner
training_progressions.focus: Linking the kneebar threat to heel hook redirect based on defensive reactions
training_progressions.description: Partner alternates between straightening leg (requiring kneebar pressure) and bending knee (opening heel hook). Practitioner reads the reaction and applies the appropriate attack. Moderate speed with cooperative resistance. Build the reaction-based chain until pattern recognition becomes instinctive.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Positional Sparring with Controlled Resistance
training_progressions.focus: Applying the transition against progressive resistance with safety constraints
training_progressions.description: Start in kneebar control. Attacker works the kneebar-to-heel-hook chain against an actively defending partner. Heel hook is applied at 50% speed maximum with immediate release on tap. Defender provides increasing resistance over sessions. Focus on timing and reading real defensive reactions.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 4: Live Integration and Competition Simulation
training_progressions.focus: Integrating the chain into full leg lock exchanges under realistic conditions
training_progressions.description: Full positional sparring from various leg entanglements with all submissions available. Practitioner must find kneebar control organically and execute the heel hook redirect against full resistance. Maintain strict safety protocols. Review and analyze decision-making after each round.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the heel hook from kneebar control primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The heel hook primarily attacks the knee's rotational ligaments — the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), medial collateral ligament (MCL), and lateral collateral ligament (LCL). Secondary targets include the menisci and the ankle ligaments. The rotational force transmitted through the heel creates torsion at the knee joint, which lacks structural resistance to rotation compared to extension or flexion forces.

flashcards.question: What physical indicators suggest the heel hook is approaching the breaking point?
flashcards.answer: Key indicators include feeling the opponent's knee begin to rotate involuntarily with your torque, sensing a sudden loss of muscular resistance as ligaments reach their elastic limit, and the opponent's body stiffening reflexively. In training, you must stop well before these indicators become apparent — the moment you feel the knee beginning to give rotationally, immediately reduce pressure and wait for the tap. Heel hooks cause damage before pain signals arrive.

flashcards.question: What control must be established before transitioning from kneebar to heel hook?
flashcards.answer: Before transitioning, ensure your leg entanglement prevents the opponent from rotating their hips freely, with your near-side leg hooked behind their knee or across their thigh. Your hips must remain connected to their leg, and the heel must be accessible to your hands. Your inside arm should be pre-positioned to thread under the ankle for heel capture. Never release leg control to reach for the heel — the entanglement does the controlling while the arms transition.

flashcards.question: At what point during this submission is escape no longer viable for the defender?
flashcards.answer: Escape becomes extremely difficult once the attacker has secured a locked figure-four or S-grip on the heel with elbows pinched tight, combined with strong leg entanglement preventing hip rotation. Before the grip locks, the defender can fight hands and straighten their leg. After the grip is secured and rotational pressure begins, the defender's options narrow to tapping immediately. The grip lock combined with hip control represents the true point of no return.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error when transitioning from kneebar to heel hook?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is releasing leg entanglement during the grip transition to reach for the heel. Attackers often open their legs to extend their reach, which allows the defender to extract their leg or rotate their hips freely. The correct approach is maintaining tight leg hooks throughout, using only the arms to change grip configuration while the legs continue controlling the opponent's hip movement and preventing extraction.

flashcards.question: How should you adjust your grip when the opponent's foot orientation makes the standard heel hook grip difficult?
flashcards.answer: If the heel faces away from your centerline, use your outside hand to cup the heel first, then thread your inside arm under the ankle to establish the figure-four. If the foot is tucked, apply kneebar pressure to force them to bend the knee deeper, which brings the heel into range. For stubborn foot positions, consider switching to a palm-to-palm or S-grip configuration rather than the traditional figure-four, as this requires less precise heel positioning while still generating strong rotational control.

flashcards.question: What makes the heel hook from kneebar control more dangerous than the kneebar itself?
flashcards.answer: The kneebar attacks through extension, which provides clear proprioceptive feedback — the defender feels increasing stretch and pressure, allowing time to tap before damage occurs. The heel hook attacks through rotation, which damages the ACL, MCL, and LCL with minimal pain warning. Defenders often do not perceive significant pain until structural damage has already occurred. This reduced feedback window makes the heel hook substantially more dangerous, demanding extremely slow application in training and immediate release on any tap signal.

flashcards.question: How should you set up the kneebar-to-heel-hook chain in a competition context?
flashcards.answer: In competition, commit to genuine kneebar pressure first to force the bent-knee defensive reaction. The kneebar must be a real threat, not a feint — apply enough force that the opponent must fully commit to bending their knee. As they commit to defense, redirect to the heel immediately. Time the grip change to coincide with their maximum defensive commitment, when the heel is most exposed and their attention is focused on preventing extension. The transition should feel like a continuous flow rather than two separate attacks.

defender.name: Heel Hook from Kneebar Control Defender
defender.description: Defend the heel hook from kneebar control in BJJ. Recognition cues, escape techniques, and survival strategies against this dangerous leg lock transition.
defender.overview: Defending the heel hook from kneebar control requires awareness that your kneebar defense itself creates the opening for this more dangerous submission. When you bend your knee to prevent hyperextension, you must simultaneously protect your heel from being captured. The transition window — when the attacker shifts grips from kneebar to heel hook — represents your best opportunity to escape, as their control is momentarily weakened during the grip change. Understanding this timing and having pre-planned defensive responses is essential, especially given the heel hook's capacity to cause structural damage before pain signals arrive. The defender must balance preventing the kneebar with protecting the heel, making this one of the more complex defensive scenarios in the leg lock game.
key_principles: Recognize that your bent-knee kneebar defense directly exposes your heel — defending one attack must not create another
The grip transition window is your best escape opportunity — act decisively when the attacker releases kneebar pressure to reach for the heel
Protect the heel actively by tucking your foot behind the attacker's body or between their legs where hands cannot reach
Control your own hip rotation — if a heel hook grip is established, rotate your hips in the direction of torque to relieve pressure
Tap early and without hesitation if the heel hook grip locks and rotation begins — ligament damage occurs before pain
Fight hands before the grip consolidates rather than trying to escape after the figure-four is locked
recognition_cues: Attacker's hands shift from hugging your leg tight against their chest toward threading under your ankle or cupping your heel
Reduction in linear kneebar extension pressure followed by the attacker adjusting their hip angle for a rotational attack vector
Feeling the attacker's forearm contacting the back of your heel or Achilles tendon area rather than reinforcing the kneebar grip
Attacker squeezes elbows together around your heel rather than pulling your leg toward their chest for extension

defensive_options.action: Boot defense — forcefully straighten your leg during the grip transition window to remove the heel from reach and re-expose the knee to extension rather than rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: The moment you feel the attacker's kneebar pressure release as they begin reaching for your heel — this narrow window is when their arm control is weakest
defensive_options.if_successful: Returns to kneebar defense position where you must now defend the extension threat, but you have eliminated the more dangerous heel hook
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker maintains strong leg entanglement, straightening your leg may expose you to a committed kneebar finish

defensive_options.action: Active heel protection — tuck your heel behind the attacker's body or between their legs while maintaining your bent-knee kneebar defense
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the kneebar threat and need to defend it by bending your knee, but want to prevent the heel hook redirect before it starts
defensive_options.if_successful: Neutralizes both the kneebar and heel hook simultaneously, forcing the attacker to reposition or transition to a different attack
defensive_options.risk: Focusing on heel position may compromise your kneebar defense if you lose track of the extension threat

defensive_options.action: Full leg extraction — explosively pull your entire leg free from the entanglement while the attacker's grips are transitioning
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker releases kneebar pressure to reach for the heel and their leg entanglement is momentarily loose — requires explosive movement
defensive_options.if_successful: Complete escape from the leg entanglement, recovering to a neutral or dominant position depending on scramble outcome
defensive_options.risk: If extraction fails halfway, you may end up in a worse entanglement with the attacker now having partial heel hook grip

escape_paths: Straighten leg forcefully during grip transition to prevent heel capture, then work to clear the leg entanglement entirely
Rotate hips in the direction of heel hook torque to relieve pressure, then extract leg while attacker adjusts angle
Strip attacker's hands from heel before the figure-four grip locks, using both hands to pry and peel their fingers

favorable_outcomes.how: Explode out of the leg entanglement during the grip transition window when the attacker's control is weakest, then consolidate top position before they can re-engage
Successfully defend the heel hook redirect by tucking heel or straightening leg, returning to standard kneebar defense where extension threat is more manageable

common_errors.error: Waiting to feel pain before tapping to the heel hook
common_errors.consequence: ACL, MCL, or LCL damage occurs before significant pain is felt, potentially requiring surgical reconstruction and 6-12 months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately when you feel rotational pressure on your knee that you cannot relieve by rotating your hips. Do not wait for pain — the absence of pain does not mean the submission is not working

common_errors.error: Defending only the kneebar without protecting the heel, leaving the foot floating freely when knee is bent
common_errors.consequence: Attacker easily transitions to heel hook because the heel is completely exposed and accessible, turning your kneebar defense into a heel hook setup
common_errors.correction: When bending your knee to defend the kneebar, actively tuck your heel behind the attacker's body or squeeze your foot between their legs where their hands cannot reach it

common_errors.error: Attempting to grip fight the heel hook after the figure-four is already locked and torque has begun
common_errors.consequence: Wasted effort that delays the tap while the attacker continues applying rotational pressure, increasing the risk of ligament damage during the time spent fighting a locked grip
common_errors.correction: Fight hands early during the grip transition, before the figure-four locks. Once the grip is secured with elbows pinched and rotation starts, your only safe option is to tap immediately

common_errors.error: Panicking and attempting explosive movements without a clear escape plan
common_errors.consequence: Random explosive movement with a partially locked heel hook grip can cause self-inflicted knee damage as the leg torques against the attacker's locked arms
common_errors.correction: Have a pre-planned defensive response for each phase of the transition. Move deliberately with purpose — either straighten the leg, rotate the hips in a specific direction, or extract with a clear path

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that your opponent is transitioning from kneebar to heel hook?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include feeling their hands shift from hugging your leg tight against their chest toward threading under your ankle or cupping your heel. You will also notice a reduction in linear extension pressure followed by the attacker adjusting their hip angle. Their forearm contacting the back of your heel or Achilles tendon rather than reinforcing the kneebar grip is the clearest signal that the heel hook redirect has begun.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to a heel hook from kneebar control to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel rotational pressure on your knee that you cannot counter by rotating your hips in the same direction. Do not wait for pain — heel hooks cause ligament damage before pain signals arrive. If the attacker has a locked grip on your heel with elbows tight and begins any rotational movement you cannot neutralize, tap immediately. It is far better to tap early and train again tomorrow than to suffer an ACL tear requiring months of rehabilitation.

flashcards.question: What are the primary defensive techniques against the heel hook from kneebar control?
flashcards.answer: Three primary defenses exist: First, straighten your leg forcefully during the grip transition window to prevent the attacker from capturing your heel and restore kneebar defense positioning. Second, rotate your hips in the same direction as the heel hook torque to relieve rotational pressure on your knee. Third, fight the heel grip actively before it locks by pulling your foot free, prying their hands apart, or tucking your heel behind their body where they cannot access it.

flashcards.question: Why is the grip transition from kneebar to heel hook a critical defensive window?
flashcards.answer: During the grip transition, the attacker must release their standard kneebar arm configuration and re-grip the heel, momentarily reducing their control strength. This creates a brief window where arm control is compromised and only the leg entanglement is maintaining position. An explosive leg straightening or hip escape during this window has the highest success probability because the attacker cannot simultaneously maintain kneebar pressure and secure the heel hook grip.

flashcards.question: What proactive measures can you take to prevent the kneebar-to-heel-hook transition entirely?
flashcards.answer: The most effective prevention is to keep your heel tucked tight behind the attacker's body or between their legs where their hands cannot reach while defending the kneebar. Maintain active foot position — never let your heel float freely when your knee is bent in defense. Additionally, work to escape the entire leg entanglement rather than defending individual submissions one at a time, as the positional escape eliminates all submission threats simultaneously and returns you to a safe position.

training_progressions.focus: Learning to identify the kneebar-to-heel-hook transition and developing safe tapping habits
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly demonstrates the grip transition from kneebar to heel hook while defender identifies each recognition cue verbally. Practice tapping at the correct moment — when the heel grip locks and rotation begins. Zero resistance, purely educational. Build automatic tap response to rotational knee pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Developing grip prevention and heel protection during the transition window
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the heel hook redirect at 50% speed while defender practices stripping grips, tucking the heel, and straightening the leg at the correct timing. Moderate resistance from both sides. Focus on reading the transition moment and selecting the appropriate defensive response.

training_progressions.focus: Executing complete escapes from kneebar control when heel hook transitions are threatened
training_progressions.description: Full positional sparring starting in kneebar control with attacker working the heel hook chain. Defender works complete escape sequences including boot defense, hip rotation, and full leg extraction. Increasing resistance with maintained safety protocols. Heel hooks applied at controlled speed only.

training_progressions.focus: Applying defensive skills under realistic conditions with full leg lock exchanges
training_progressions.description: Open leg lock sparring where kneebar-to-heel-hook transitions occur organically. Defender must recognize and respond to transitions in real time with full resistance. Maintain strict safety protocols throughout. Debrief after each round to analyze decision points and defensive timing.
